title: Modi Is in Indonesia With a Missile Deal. Then He'll Face a Million Indians in Melbourne and Anti-Indian Sentiment in New Zealand.
excerpt: A six-day, three-nation tour through the Asia-Pacific puts defence exports, temple diplomacy, and diaspora politics on the same itinerary.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Modi's Asia-Pacific tour includes Indonesia, Australia, and New Zealand over six days.
  • A key focus is finalizing a $200-$350 million BrahMos missile deal with Indonesia.
  • Modi will announce a restoration project for Prambanan temple, strengthening cultural ties.
  • Australia hosts one million Indian-born residents, making Modi's visit significant domestically.
  • Modi's New Zealand visit is the first in 40 years amid rising anti-Indian sentiment.

Sources: Reuters, Ministry of External Affairs (India)
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Jakarta on Monday for the first leg of an ambitious three-nation tour through the Asia-Pacific, with Indonesia, Australia, and New Zealand on the itinerary over the next six days. It is the most consequential Indian diplomatic push into the region this year — and for the nearly four million Indians living across these three countries, every stop carries weight. The centrepiece of the Indonesia visit is a high-stakes meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, where the two leaders are expected to finalise agreements on defence, food security, space cooperation, and pharmaceuticals. But the headline item is BrahMos — the supersonic cruise missile jointly developed by India and Russia that has become New Delhi's most potent defence export. ## BrahMos and a Shifting Defence Map India's ambassador to Indonesia, Sandeep Chakravorty, confirmed last week that the two countries hope to "conclude certain agreements" on BrahMos during the visit. A deal — estimated at between $200 million and $350 million — would make Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer of the missile system, after the Philippines and Vietnam. For India, BrahMos sales are more than revenue. They are a statement that New Delhi can be a credible defence supplier in a region where China's military footprint is expanding rapidly. Prabowo, a former military commander himself, has been modernising Indonesia's armed forces since taking office and has signalled interest in diversifying away from Western suppliers. ![Prime Minister Narendra Modi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/The_official_portrait_of_Shri_Narendra_Modi%2C_the_Prime_Minister_of_the_Republic_of_India.jpg) > **"It is the most consequential Indian diplomatic push into the region this year — and for the nearly four million Indians living across these three countries, every stop carries weight."** The defence talks will also cover maritime domain awareness and anti-piracy cooperation — areas where the two countries' interests overlap heavily given their shared dependence on shipping lanes through the Indian Ocean and the Malacca Strait. ## Restoring a Hindu Temple, Building a Cultural Bridge In a move that will resonate with the Indian diaspora worldwide, Modi announced he would visit Prambanan — Indonesia's largest Hindu temple complex and a UNESCO World Heritage site — in Yogyakarta. Both leaders are expected to announce the start of a joint restoration project at the ninth-century site. The gesture is significant. Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim-majority nation, is home to a rich Hindu heritage that predates Islam's arrival. For Indian-origin communities across Southeast Asia, Prambanan is a powerful symbol of civilisational ties that transcend modern borders. ## Food Security and Palm Oil Beyond defence and culture, the visit addresses bread-and-butter economic concerns. India is one of Indonesia's largest buyers of palm oil and coal. Jakarta's recent decision to centralise control over strategic commodity exports — a move that spooked some trading partners — will be on the table. Chakravorty struck a diplomatic note: "We understand the reasons and we believe that we are part of the solution." New agreements on food security and pharmaceutical supply chains are expected to formalise what has been an increasingly intertwined economic relationship. ![New Delhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg/3840px-Forecourt%2C_Rashtrapati_Bhavan_-_1.jpg)

## Australia and the Diaspora Question From Indonesia, Modi heads to Melbourne for the third India-Australia Annual Summit with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Australia's one million Indian-born residents — now the country's largest overseas-born population — make this a visit with domestic resonance on both sides. Officials have been scouting Melbourne venues with capacities of up to 35,000 for a community event, and Modi is expected to visit the Melbourne Cricket Ground — a pilgrimage site of a different kind for the cricket-mad diaspora. ## New Zealand: First Visit in 40 Years The final stop, New Zealand, is perhaps the most politically delicate. Modi's visit — the first by an Indian prime minister in four decades — comes amid rising anti-Indian sentiment in the country. A free-trade agreement signed in April is causing friction within New Zealand's ruling coalition, and community leaders will be watching closely to see whether the visit calms or inflames the debate.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has called the visit "historic." For the roughly 250,000 people of Indian origin in New Zealand, it is overdue. *Sources: Reuters, Ministry of External Affairs (India), The Australia Today*
